chapter: On the road and into brass bands
title: The Sawdust and Chitlin' Circuit
summary: Explains the Sawdust Circuit, named for sawdust spread on damp club floors, in a time of no halls for black musicians.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Well, y'all were obviously on the road.

Oh, yeah, we were on the road. Yeah, we were on the road with Champion Jack Dupree. And then later on, about a month or two later from that, we came into Jimmy Witherspoon. Jimmy Witherspoon, Jimmy Liggins, Joe Liggins. Like I said, we were working for this guy out of Atlanta. Henry, something. And he used to do shows like that.
So y'all were just on a circuit?
Yeah, we call it the Sawdust Circuit.
Sawdust. Yeah. Referred to as Sawdust.
Well, because these places we played, and another name for it is the Chitlin's.

Well, the Sawdust is because a lot of the places we played and so forth, the places were all damp and so forth and so on. And for the dance, they spread a lot of sawdust on the floor. So people would be dancing in Sawdust and not in the sort of wet damp flows that they had in these clubs for us to play. A barn type thing, you know, or something. In those days you didn't play in the auditoriums and the Hilton's and all that kind of stuff. There was no such thing. And there was no such thing for black musicians to play in. So we played the Chitlin's Circuit, the Chitlin's Circuit, or the Sawdust Circuit.
Yeah, the club on the other side of the track.
